title: Kaizen
author: Masaaki Imai
theme: Lasting competitive strength comes from small, continuous improvements made by everyone, every day, rather than from occasional dramatic breakthroughs.
summary: Masaaki Imai wrote this book to explain to Western readers why so many Japanese companies had become formidable competitors. His answer is a single idea: kaizen, a Japanese word for gradual, ongoing improvement that involves everyone in the organisation, from senior managers to workers on the shop floor.

Imai contrasts kaizen with innovation. Western firms, he argues, tended to rely on big leaps, such as new technology, major investment or a reorganisation, and then let performance slowly decay until the next leap. Kaizen works differently. It is a steady stream of small, low-cost changes that keeps standards rising between breakthroughs. The two approaches are complementary, but the incremental one is often neglected.

In his view, management has two jobs. Maintenance means setting standards and making sure people follow them. Improvement means raising those standards. The higher a manager sits, the more time should go to improvement, while frontline staff spend more of their effort on maintaining and refining daily work.

A central theme is process orientation. Rather than judging people only by results, managers should pay attention to the methods, effort and discipline that produce results, because better processes lead to better outcomes over time. Improvement follows the plan-do-check-act cycle, and once a gain is achieved it is locked in as a new standard.

Imai treats quality as the first priority and asks people to argue with data rather than opinion. He extends the idea of the customer inside the firm: each step should treat the next step as its customer and pass on no defects.

Kaizen, he says, is an umbrella covering many familiar practices, including company-wide quality control, just-in-time production, suggestion systems, small-group activities and policy deployment from top management.
The book's message is that improvement is a habit and a culture, not a project with an end date.
takeaway: Make small improvements every day, focus on processes as well as results, and turn each gain into a new standard.

questions.q: What does the word 'kaizen' mean in Imai's book?
options: A sudden technological breakthrough
Gradual, continuous improvement involving everyone
A cost-cutting programme led by consultants
A system of performance bonuses
questions.why: Imai defines kaizen as ongoing, incremental improvement in which everyone in the organisation takes part.

questions.q: How does Imai contrast kaizen with innovation?
options: Innovation is cheap and kaizen is expensive
They are the same thing under different names
Kaizen is small and continuous, while innovation comes in large, occasional leaps
Innovation involves everyone, while kaizen involves only experts
questions.why: He presents innovation as dramatic step changes and kaizen as a steady flow of small improvements between them.

questions.q: According to Imai, what tends to happen after a major innovation if there is no kaizen?
options: Performance gradually slips back as standards decay
Performance keeps rising automatically
Costs fall to zero
Workers stop needing any standards
questions.why: Without ongoing maintenance and improvement, the gains from a breakthrough erode over time.

questions.q: What are the two main functions of management in the book?
options: Hiring and firing
Budgeting and forecasting
Marketing and sales
Maintenance and improvement
questions.why: Imai says managers must both uphold current standards and work to raise them.

questions.q: How should the balance between maintenance and improvement change with seniority?
options: Senior managers should focus only on maintenance
Higher-level managers should devote more of their time to improvement
Everyone should spend equal time on both
Only frontline workers should improve anything
questions.why: In his model, the share of effort given to improvement grows as one moves up the hierarchy.

questions.q: What does 'process orientation' ask managers to do?
options: Ignore results completely
Judge staff solely on final numbers
Pay attention to the methods and effort that produce results, not only the results
Replace all processes with automation
questions.why: Imai argues that improving the process is the reliable path to better results over time.

questions.q: Which cycle does Imai describe as the engine of improvement?
options: Plan-do-check-act
Buy-build-sell-repeat
Hire-train-review-promote
Forecast-budget-spend-audit
questions.why: The plan-do-check-act cycle is used to test changes and keep improving step by step.

questions.q: What should happen once an improvement has been achieved?
options: It should be kept secret from other teams
It should be reversed at the next review
It should be left to individuals to follow if they wish
It should become the new standard for the work
questions.why: Standardising each gain prevents backsliding and creates the base for the next improvement.

questions.q: What does treating 'the next process as the customer' mean?
options: Sending defects downstream for others to fix
Each step should deliver defect-free work to the step that follows it
Charging internal departments for services
Letting external customers design every process
questions.why: Imai extends customer thinking inside the firm so that no step passes problems on to the next.

questions.q: Which of these does Imai place under the 'kaizen umbrella'?
options: Hostile takeovers
Annual layoffs
Company-wide quality control, just-in-time production and suggestion systems
Outsourcing all production
questions.why: He presents many Japanese management practices, including quality control, just-in-time and suggestion systems, as expressions of kaizen.
